name: Frog
title: Frog Atlas
blurb: Rana tigrina, the Indian bullfrog of school biology: skeleton, three-chambered heart, lungs, gut and urogenital system.

parts.name: Skull
parts.d: A broad, flat and lightweight skull. Unlike ours it has large open orbits and few bones, and it joins the spine through two occipital condyles (dicondylic).
parts.fn: Protects the small brain, supports the huge eyes and forms the upper jaw, which carries tiny maxillary teeth for gripping prey.
parts.kid: A frog's skull is flat and full of big holes for its bulging eyes.

parts.name: Lower Jaw
parts.d: A U-shaped jaw of several small bones (dentary, angulosplenial and mentomeckelian). It has no teeth.
parts.fn: Hinges widely so the frog can swallow prey whole; the sticky tongue is attached at its front.
parts.kid: Frogs have no teeth in their bottom jaw — they swallow their food whole.

parts.name: Atlas (Vertebra 1)
parts.d: The first vertebra, with no transverse processes, carrying the skull on two cup-shaped facets.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 2
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 3
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 4
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 5
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 6
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 7
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Vertebra 8
parts.d: One of the procoelous vertebrae of the short frog spine — there are only nine vertebrae plus the urostyle, and no ribs.
parts.fn: Protects the spinal cord and gives the trunk a short, rigid frame for leaping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Sacral Vertebra (Vertebra 9)
parts.d: The ninth vertebra, whose large transverse processes articulate with the long ilia of the pelvic girdle.
parts.fn: Transfers the thrust of the hind legs to the spine during jumping.
parts.kid: A frog has only 9 back bones — and no ribs at all!

parts.name: Urostyle
parts.d: A long, rod-like bone formed by fused tail vertebrae, running back from the sacral vertebra between the ilia.
parts.fn: Stiffens the rear of the body and anchors muscles used in jumping — a reminder that the tadpole had a tail.
parts.kid: This bone is what's left of the tadpole's tail.

parts.name: Suprascapula
parts.d: A broad, partly cartilaginous plate forming the upper part of the shoulder girdle over the back.
parts.fn: Anchors the shoulder muscles and braces the forelimbs.
parts.kid: Frogs land on their arms, so their shoulder bones act like shock absorbers.

parts.name: Scapula
parts.d: A short bone joining the suprascapula to the glenoid cavity.
parts.fn: Forms the upper half of the shoulder socket.
parts.kid: Frogs land on their arms, so their shoulder bones act like shock absorbers.

parts.name: Clavicle
parts.d: A slender bar running from the midline to the shoulder at the front of the girdle.
parts.fn: Braces the shoulder against the sternum when the frog lands.
parts.kid: Frogs land on their arms, so their shoulder bones act like shock absorbers.

parts.name: Coracoid
parts.d: A stout bone behind the clavicle joining the girdle to the ventral midline.
parts.fn: Takes the impact of landing on the forelimbs.
parts.kid: Frogs land on their arms, so their shoulder bones act like shock absorbers.

parts.name: Sternum
parts.d: The frog's breastbone — the omosternum in front and sternum behind the girdle — with no ribs attached.
parts.fn: Anchors the chest muscles and ties the two halves of the pectoral girdle together.
parts.kid: Frogs have a breastbone but no ribs.

parts.name: Humerus
parts.d: The upper arm bone, with a prominent crest (deltoid ridge) in males for gripping females during mating.
parts.fn: Carries the forelimb muscles that cushion landing after a jump.
parts.kid: Frogs' strong back legs let them jump up to 20 times their own body length.

parts.name: Radio-ulna
parts.d: The radius and ulna fused into a single bone, with a groove showing where they joined.
parts.fn: Forms the rigid forearm that props the front of the body up.
parts.kid: Frogs' strong back legs let them jump up to 20 times their own body length.

parts.name: Femur
parts.d: The long, slightly S-shaped thigh bone.
parts.fn: Carries the powerful thigh muscles that straighten the leg in a jump.
parts.kid: Frogs' strong back legs let them jump up to 20 times their own body length.

parts.name: Tibio-fibula
parts.d: The tibia and fibula fused into one long bone, longer than the femur.
parts.fn: Adds a long lever to the hind leg for jumping and swimming.
parts.kid: Frogs' strong back legs let them jump up to 20 times their own body length.

parts.name: Astragalus & Calcaneum
parts.d: Two elongated ankle bones (tarsals), fused at each end, forming an extra segment of the leg.
parts.fn: Give the frog a fourth leg segment for extra leverage when leaping.
parts.kid: Frogs' strong back legs let them jump up to 20 times their own body length.

parts.name: Hand Bones
parts.d: The carpals, metacarpals and phalanges of the hand. The frog has four fingers; the thumb is only a vestige.
parts.fn: Spread on the ground to steady the body and, in males, grip the female during mating (amplexus).
parts.kid: Frogs have 4 fingers on each hand but 5 toes on each foot.

parts.name: Foot Bones
parts.d: The metatarsals and phalanges of the five long, webbed toes.
parts.fn: Support the webbing that makes the hind feet powerful paddles for swimming.
parts.kid: Webbed feet work like flippers.

parts.name: Ilium
parts.d: A long rod-like bone running from the sacral vertebra back to the acetabulum — the frog's hips are stretched out for jumping.
parts.fn: Transmits the kick of the hind legs forward to the spine.
parts.kid: A frog's hip bones are long rods that act like the springs in a catapult.

parts.name: Ischium & Pubis
parts.d: The fused ischium and (cartilaginous) pubis forming a disc at the back of the pelvis with the socket for each femur.
parts.fn: Holds the hip sockets (acetabula) where the legs attach.
parts.kid: The hip sockets are at the very back of the frog.

parts.name: Gastrocnemius
parts.d: The big calf muscle of the frog, ending in the tendon of Achilles over the ankle.
parts.fn: Straightens the ankle to power jumping and swimming. Galvani's famous 1780s experiments on frog legs used this muscle.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Triceps Femoris
parts.d: The large three-part muscle on the front of the thigh.
parts.fn: Straightens the knee during the jump.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Sartorius
parts.d: A long, thin strap across the underside of the thigh.
parts.fn: Bends the knee and pulls the thigh forward.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Gluteus
parts.d: A muscle over the ilium at the hip.
parts.fn: Pulls the thigh forward and outward.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Pectoralis
parts.d: A fan-shaped chest muscle on the underside.
parts.fn: Pulls the forelimb inward and backward.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Deltoid
parts.d: A shoulder muscle over the humerus.
parts.fn: Moves the forelimb forward.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Rectus Abdominis
parts.d: A long band along the belly with transverse tendinous lines.
parts.fn: Supports the abdominal organs and bends the body.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: External Oblique
parts.d: A thin sheet of muscle on the side of the trunk.
parts.fn: Compresses the abdomen, helping to push air out of the lungs.
parts.kid: Frog leg muscles are among the most studied muscles in science.

parts.name: Mylohyoid
parts.d: A sheet of muscle across the floor of the mouth.
parts.fn: Raises and lowers the floor of the mouth in 'buccal pumping' — the way a frog pushes air into its lungs, since it has no diaphragm.
parts.kid: Watch a frog's throat pump up and down — that's how it breathes!

parts.name: Ventricle
parts.d: The single, thick-walled, conical ventricle of the frog's three-chambered heart.
parts.fn: Pumps blood into the truncus arteriosus. Because there is only one ventricle, oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood partly mix.
parts.kid: A frog's heart has 3 rooms. Yours has 4!

parts.name: Right Atrium
parts.d: The larger of the two atria, receiving blood from the sinus venosus.
parts.fn: Collects deoxygenated blood returning from the body.
parts.kid: Blood from the body comes back into this chamber.

parts.name: Left Atrium
parts.d: The smaller atrium, receiving oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein.
parts.fn: Passes oxygen-rich blood into the ventricle.
parts.kid: Blood from the lungs comes into this chamber.

parts.name: Sinus Venosus
parts.d: A triangular thin-walled chamber on the back of the heart, formed by the joining of the venae cavae.
parts.fn: Collects blood from the body and passes it to the right atrium; the heartbeat starts here.
parts.kid: Every heartbeat starts in this little sac.

parts.name: Truncus Arteriosus
parts.d: A tube-like chamber leaving the front of the ventricle, containing a spiral valve.
parts.fn: Directs blood into the three pairs of aortic arches; its spiral valve helps keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood partly separate.
parts.kid: The main pipe leaving a frog's heart splits into three pairs of arches.

parts.name: Carotid Arch
parts.d: The front pair of aortic arches, running forward into the head.
parts.fn: Supplies the head and brain.
parts.kid: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

parts.name: Systemic Arch
parts.d: The middle pair of arches, which curve back and join above the gut to form the dorsal aorta.
parts.fn: Carries blood to the body and forelimbs.
parts.kid: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

parts.name: Pulmocutaneous Arch
parts.d: The hind pair of arches, dividing into pulmonary and cutaneous arteries.
parts.fn: Takes blood to the lungs and the skin to collect oxygen — both are breathing surfaces in a frog.
parts.kid: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

parts.name: Dorsal Aorta
parts.d: The main artery running back along the roof of the body cavity.
parts.fn: Supplies the gut, kidneys, gonads and hind legs.
parts.kid: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

meta.Formed: Union of the two systemic arches

parts.name: Postcaval Vein
parts.d: A large vein running forward from the kidneys through the liver to the sinus venosus.
parts.fn: Returns blood from the kidneys, liver and hind body to the heart.
parts.kid: Veins bring blood back to the heart.

parts.name: Precaval Vein
parts.d: One of a pair of veins from the head and forelimbs.
parts.fn: Returns blood from the front of the body to the sinus venosus.
parts.kid: Veins bring blood back to the heart.

parts.name: Hepatic Portal Vein
parts.d: Carries blood from the intestine to the liver.
parts.fn: Lets the liver process food absorbed from the gut before it reaches the heart.
parts.kid: Veins bring blood back to the heart.

parts.name: Renal Portal Vein
parts.d: Carries blood from the hind legs into the kidney. Frogs, unlike mammals, have a renal portal system.
parts.fn: Brings blood from the lower body to the kidneys for filtering.
parts.kid: Veins bring blood back to the heart.

parts.name: Lung
parts.d: A pair of thin, elastic, sac-like lungs with a honeycomb of shallow chambers inside.
parts.fn: Used for breathing on land; air is forced in by buccal pumping. Underwater and during hibernation the frog breathes through its moist skin instead.
parts.kid: Frogs breathe with lungs AND through their skin!

parts.name: Larynx
parts.d: A small voice box behind the mouth, with vocal cords.
parts.fn: Produces the frog's croaking calls.
parts.kid: Frogs croak to call each other.

parts.name: Vocal Sac
parts.d: A thin balloon of skin at each corner of the male's mouth.
parts.fn: Inflates to amplify the male's mating call — a feature of sexual dimorphism in frogs.
parts.kid: Male frogs blow up these bubbles to croak loudly.

parts.name: Tongue
parts.d: A sticky, muscular tongue attached at the FRONT of the mouth, with a forked (bilobed) free end pointing back.
parts.fn: Flips out in a fraction of a second to catch insects, then carries them back into the mouth.
parts.kid: A frog's tongue is attached at the front and flips out to catch bugs!

parts.name: Oesophagus
parts.d: A short, wide tube from the pharynx to the stomach.
parts.fn: Moves swallowed prey quickly into the stomach.
parts.kid: Food slides down this short tube.

parts.name: Stomach
parts.d: A curved, J-shaped sac on the left side of the body cavity.
parts.fn: Stores prey and begins protein digestion with hydrochloric acid and pepsin.
parts.kid: Frogs swallow bugs whole and digest them in their stomach.

parts.name: Small Intestine
parts.d: The coiled duodenum and ileum, held in place by mesentery.
parts.fn: Completes digestion with bile and pancreatic juice and absorbs the nutrients into the blood.
parts.kid: Food is broken down and soaked up in this long coiled tube.

parts.name: Rectum
parts.d: The wide last part of the gut (large intestine).
parts.fn: Absorbs water and stores faeces before they pass into the cloaca.
parts.kid: Waste waits here before it leaves the body.

parts.name: Cloaca
parts.d: A single chamber at the end of the body into which the gut, kidneys and reproductive ducts all open.
parts.fn: Passes out faeces, urine, eggs or sperm through one opening, the vent.
parts.kid: Frogs have one opening for poo, pee and eggs.

parts.name: Liver
parts.d: A large, reddish-brown gland of three lobes (right, left and median) lying around the heart and stomach.
parts.fn: Makes bile, stores glycogen and fat, and processes nutrients from the gut.
parts.kid: The liver is the largest gland in a frog.

parts.name: Gall Bladder
parts.d: A small greenish sac between the lobes of the liver.
parts.fn: Stores bile, which it releases into the duodenum to emulsify fats.
parts.kid: It stores green bile for digesting fat.

parts.name: Pancreas
parts.d: A thin, pale gland in the loop between the stomach and duodenum.
parts.fn: Secretes digestive enzymes into the duodenum and hormones (insulin, glucagon) into the blood.
parts.kid: The pancreas helps digest food and controls blood sugar.

parts.name: Spleen
parts.d: A small, round, dark-red organ in the mesentery near the rectum.
parts.fn: Stores and filters blood and produces lymphocytes.
parts.kid: A tiny round organ that filters blood.

parts.name: Kidney
parts.d: A pair of long, flat, dark-red kidneys lying against the back of the body cavity.
parts.fn: Filter waste from the blood and make urine. Frogs are ureotelic — they excrete nitrogen mainly as urea.
parts.kid: A frog's kidneys clean its blood, just like yours.

parts.name: Ureter
parts.d: A thin tube from each kidney to the cloaca. In males it also carries sperm (urinogenital duct).
parts.fn: Carries urine to the cloaca.
parts.kid: Pee travels down these tubes.

parts.name: Urinary Bladder
parts.d: A thin-walled, two-lobed sac attached to the cloaca.
parts.fn: Stores urine and lets the frog reabsorb water when it is on dry land.
parts.kid: Frogs store water in their bladder in case they get dry.

parts.name: Fat Body
parts.d: Yellow, finger-shaped bodies attached near the gonads.
parts.fn: Store fat that fuels the frog through hibernation and the breeding season.
parts.kid: Frogs store fat here to survive the winter.

parts.name: Testis
parts.d: A yellowish oval body attached to the front of each kidney by a fold of peritoneum.
parts.fn: Produces sperm, which pass through vasa efferentia into the kidney and out along the urinogenital duct.
parts.kid: The testes make sperm cells.

parts.name: Ovary
parts.d: A large, lobed ovary on each side, packed with black-and-white eggs in the breeding season.
parts.fn: Produces 2 500–3 000 eggs at a time, which are laid in water and fertilised externally.
parts.kid: A frog can lay thousands of eggs at once!

parts.name: Oviduct
parts.d: A long, coiled tube running from near the lungs to the cloaca.
parts.fn: Coats the eggs in jelly as they pass towards the cloaca.
parts.kid: Eggs get their jelly coat in this tube.

parts.name: Olfactory Lobes
parts.d: The small paired lobes at the very front of the brain.
parts.fn: Process the sense of smell.
parts.kid: A frog's brain is tiny, but it has the same main parts as yours.

parts.name: Cerebral Hemispheres
parts.d: Two elongated hemispheres forming most of the forebrain.
parts.fn: Handle smell-related and simple learned behaviour.
parts.kid: A frog's brain is tiny, but it has the same main parts as yours.

parts.name: Optic Lobes
parts.d: A pair of rounded lobes forming the roof of the midbrain.
parts.fn: Process vision — the frog's most important sense for catching prey.
parts.kid: A frog's brain is tiny, but it has the same main parts as yours.

parts.name: Cerebellum
parts.d: A narrow band across the hindbrain behind the optic lobes; small in frogs.
parts.fn: Coordinates movement and balance.
parts.kid: A frog's brain is tiny, but it has the same main parts as yours.

parts.name: Medulla Oblongata
parts.d: The rear of the brain, continuous with the spinal cord through the foramen magnum.
parts.fn: Controls breathing, heartbeat and other automatic functions. Ten pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain.
parts.kid: A frog's brain is tiny, but it has the same main parts as yours.

parts.name: Spinal Cord
parts.d: The nerve cord running through the short vertebral column, giving off ten pairs of spinal nerves.
parts.fn: Relays messages between the brain and body and controls reflexes.
parts.kid: Messages travel up and down this cord.

parts.name: Sciatic Nerve
parts.d: The large nerve of the hind leg.
parts.fn: Controls the muscles of the leg used in jumping and swimming.
parts.kid: This nerve makes the frog's legs kick.

parts.name: Brachial Nerve
parts.d: The main nerve of the forelimb.
parts.fn: Controls the arm muscles.
parts.kid: This nerve moves the frog's arms.

parts.name: Eye
parts.d: A large, bulging eye on top of the head, protected by a see-through third eyelid, the nictitating membrane.
parts.fn: Gives a wide field of view to spot prey and predators while the frog sits almost submerged. The eyes also sink down to help push food down the throat.
parts.kid: Frogs use their eyes to help swallow — they push them down into their mouth!

parts.name: Tympanum
parts.d: The round eardrum on the side of the head behind each eye. Frogs have no outer ear.
parts.fn: Receives sound vibrations, which the columella bone carries to the inner ear.
parts.kid: That round circle behind a frog's eye is its eardrum.

parts.name: Skin
parts.d: Smooth, slippery skin kept moist by mucous glands, with no scales. The back is olive-green with dark spots; the belly is pale.
parts.fn: A breathing surface (cutaneous respiration), especially underwater and during hibernation. Frogs do not drink — they absorb water through the skin. It also changes colour for camouflage.
parts.kid: Frogs drink water through their skin instead of their mouth!
